paragraphs.en: I [[have]] [[never]] been good at starting over, so moving to a small [[country]] town at thirty-four felt [[bold]] and foolish at once.
The paper's [[newsroom]] sat above a [[newsstand]], and my new colleagues gave me a [[decent]] desk by the window.
They said the town was [[open]] to [[newcomers|newcomer]], though older residents still [[weighed|weigh]] every accent and every pair of shoes.
My first assignment was to cover a [[marine]] research station that had just opened on the coast.
Public interest in the project was [[never]] strong, and the station's work had little [[impact]] on daily life.
Behind the [[counter]] of the station's small cafe worked a man in his sixties who had once lived in a [[counterculture]] commune.
He told me the commune had tried to live on [[raw]] vegetables and open conversation, and that both had proved harder than expected.
He had a [[gift]] for describing failure without self-pity, and I liked him at once.
His stories had a [[far-reaching]] effect on the way I saw the town.
I asked if he ever missed that life, and he said [[never]] for a day.
The station's director [[led|lead]] me through a corridor of tanks and pipes, and explained that her [[subfield]] of [[marine]] biology had changed completely in ten years.
[[Part]] of the work was public education, and part was pure research with no clear product.
She was [[tempted|tempt]] to take an industry grant, but the terms would have tied her data to a company's interests.
The lab was half [[underground]], and the air smelled of salt and electricity.
A recent [[amendment]] to the funding rules had made such deals harder, which she counted as a small [[victory]].
Against the [[backdrop]] of the harbour, the old [[campus]] looked more like a [[hotel]] than a school.
A [[block]] of [[new]] flats had been built on the land where the [[library]] once stood.

The director tried to [[coax]] the council into funding a new lab, but the meeting produced nothing; the [[creation]] of the station had already cost a fortune, and the expense was [[devastating]] for a town this small.
Her questions were designed to [[elicit]] facts, not to trap anyone, and she treated every rumour as a possible [[falsehood]].
With her [[foresight]], she had saved the station's records before the flood, and I [[envied|envy]] that kind of patience.
The station's status was [[government-defined]], which meant its budget could change with every election, and its mission was [[distinct]] from the university's, though the two shared a laboratory.
That dependence produced a constant [[insecurity]], and a [[lawsuit]] against a former supplier only made things worse.
The most [[lucrative]] contract had gone to a firm that promised to turn seaweed into fuel.
Reaching a [[million]] samples had been a [[milestone]], but the celebration was a [[packed]] room full of [[onion]] soup and paper plates.
Someone had left a [[pile]] of dishes in the sink, and nobody wanted to wash them.
A [[renowned]] [[architect]] designed the new wing, and he arrived on campus with a portfolio and an assistant.
His plan [[presupposed|presuppose]] that the town would grow, which everyone doubted.
He spoke to a group of [[pupils|pupil]] from the local [[school]] and asked them what a building should do; his answer was [[reliance]] on light and air, not on expensive machines.
The council chose to [[invest]] [[slowly|slow]], one [[step]] at a time, and the architect [[swallowed|swallow]] his disappointment.
He had never wanted a [[throne]] of his own, he said, only a building that people would use.
On weekends I played the [[traveller]], taking the bus into the [[countryside]] with a notebook and a bottle of water.
The service was [[unpopular]] with local people, but it [[carried|carry]] students and farmers alike.
A [[vocal]] group had campaigned for a new line, [[whereby]] the bus would [[reach]] the [[farther]] villages.
The [[commission]] met in the old station building, where an iron [[bed]] frame still stood in the corner.
The [[elite]] of the town ignored the debate, and the rest simply waited.

My editor had a habit of [[hawking|hawk]] his own opinions as if they were headlines, and when a [[leak]] appeared in the council's budget he [[giggled|giggle]] and said the truth always finds a door.
He [[marked|mark]] the passage in red and told me to follow it up, which I did the next morning.
The [[newly]] elected mayor was a fan of [[opera]], and her first speech quoted an aria nobody knew.
Her plan received only [[partial]] support, and the [[subsequent]] debate [[tended|tend]] to drift into personal insults.
It was a [[weird]] week, and I [[learned|learn]] more from the arguments than from the documents.
At [[nightfall]] a [[couple]] from the newsroom took me to a bar where the owner [[carved|carve]] his name into the wall.
They told me that [[courage]] in this job means asking the question everyone [[else]] is avoiding.
I [[decided|decide]] to try it the next day, and the [[haze]] over the harbour made the [[market]] look like a painting.
The smell of [[newsprint]] and coffee [[gave|give]] the office a comfortable gravity.
My colleague [[leaned|lean]] across the table, said the town's only [[vice]] was gossip, and told me I would learn to love it.
The station [[operated|operate]] on a budget that was, in plain terms, a [[puzzle]].
Its director [[reacted|react]] to every cut with the same calm, and never [[undermined|undermine]] a colleague in public.
A [[science]] writer added [[subtitles|subtitle]] to the station's videos, which helped the public understand the work.
The atmosphere in the room was [[tense]] when the vote was announced, and then everyone [[behaved|behave]] [[well]].
The small win was a [[victory]] for patience rather than money.
The paper paid in [[cash]] for freelance work, which suited a town with few banks.
My first [[course]] in the job was a lesson in listening, and I [[covered|cover]] three meetings a week.
A [[crack]] in the council's account was easy to see once you looked, but the explanation [[eluded|elude]] everyone.
In [[fashion]], the town was twenty years behind, and the market was still the [[marketplace]] of rumour.
The [[head]] of the council resigned, and the story ran on the front page.
The resignation was an [[opportunity]], and I was [[ready]] for it.
There was something [[subtle]] in the way the mayor avoided the word 'resign'.
Her [[success]] had been built on [[terms|term]] she never explained, and the town began to [[suffer]] for it.
I began to [[understand]] that a [[well-connected]] friend can be more useful than a good argument.
From my window I could see the harbour [[behind]] the roofs, and the [[view]] calmed me.
A [[crash]] on the coastal road kept the paper's staff busy for two days, and the story tested every [[craft]] we had.
The [[cast]] of the story included a fisherman, a delivery driver, and a visiting [[headhunter]].
The headhunter was in town to recruit engineers for an [[e-commerce]] firm, part of a national [[craze]] for online shopping.
[[Fast]] money attracted fast talk, and at [[least]] two local shops closed within a month.
My colleague announced at a [[party]] that she would [[marry]] her [[partner]] in the spring.
The [[ban]] on [[single-use]] [[cutlery]] was, in [[real]] terms, a small thing.
But its [[scope]] was wider than expected, and the [[suggestion]] of a total ban caused something close to [[terror]] in the restaurant trade.
Restaurant owners wore the same [[suit]] to every meeting, as if uniforms could win an argument.
A [[well-educated]] economist offered a different [[viewpoint]], and the debate turned on the cost of paper forks.
[[Amid]] the shouting, the ban delivered a [[blow]] to the town's confidence, and nobody could agree on a replacement.
The council's plan had a [[cap]] on spending, and the [[equation]] was simple: less money, fewer services.
A developer was accused of [[forging|forge]] signatures, and the [[law]] was slow to respond.
The scandal was a [[hindrance]] to the town's attempt to attract investment, and it caused real [[distress]] among shopkeepers; something ugly had begun to [[creep]] into local politics.
One blogger [[falsely]] claimed that the mayor had taken a bribe, which did nothing to [[incite]] calm.
The town's credit [[grade]] fell, and a summer course in [[coding]] promised to teach the new literacy to anyone with a laptop.
In the [[newsroom]], [[opinion]] was cheap and evidence was expensive.
The editor wanted a story that could [[painlessly]] [[please]] both sides, which I said was impossible.
He [[pushed|push]] me to find a third angle, and I spent the afternoon in a [[grocery]] store asking shoppers what they thought.
The [[overarching]] question was whether a town can [[enact]] a rule without punishing its own people.
A [[cynic]] on the bus told me the answer was no, and I was on the [[verge]] of agreeing.
The library had a [[photocopier]] that jammed every morning, and a computer running [[software]] nobody trusted.
My research had reached a [[plateau]], and I needed a small [[nudge]] to finish it.
The paper offered a [[premium]] for stories that could be read on a phone, and the editor wanted an [[upgrade]] to the website.
Small errors had [[accumulated|accumulate]] in the archive, and no [[algorithm]] could correct them.
With the [[advent]] of cheap storage, we could keep everything and understand less.
Rumours were [[rampant]] by Friday, and even the [[renowned]] professor from the station had heard them.
He [[snapped|snap]] his fingers and said a good reporter should be able to [[juggle]] facts without dropping any.
That weekend we took a [[trip]] to a [[geological]] [[basin]], where the rock layers were a [[landmark]] for students.
I carried a [[portable]] radio and a notebook, and the wind made writing almost impossible.
At dusk the town looked small and stubborn, and I understood why people stayed; the paper would print the story on Monday, and I would learn whether it mattered.
